title: When a good score hides a bad model
notes: 3 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: A good average can hide bad predictions. Define: Ask which cases fail before trusting one score. Walk through: Find the weak cases; explain the error pattern; change one condition; check and preserve the result. Ask: Does a good test average establish future reliability? Expected answer and boundary: No. It describes the checked observations and metric. The same questions apply to LSTM and Transformer predictions, but this lesson uses transparent synthetic regression, not real stock data. Visual purpose: show Average score > Individual errors > Error groups > Bounded conclusion. Facilitation: ask students for a prediction before execution, locate the actual intermediate values, and distinguish observation from interpretation. Transition: connect this checked mechanism to the next beat; preserve the lab artifact where requested. [Sources] https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/production-ml-systems/monitoring ; https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html ; https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html#regression-metrics. Original teaching example, not an empirical deployment claim. Cover artwork: /assets/week09/visual-provenance.json. Quantitative images: current week notebook execution record. Revision clarification: complete Tasks 1 to 8 in a single notebook. The fixed horizontal five-point illustration is not fitted. Compare real residuals on shared scales. CSV readback is same-kernel only.

title: Count the weak cases, not just the average
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: Count the weak cases, not just the average. Define: A small difficult group can be hidden by many easy cases. Walk through: Ninety absolute errors of 1 and ten of 10 give total absolute error 190 across 100 cases. These are illustrative errors, not fitted-model measurements. Ask: What information is missing from an average of 1.9? Expected answer and boundary: The group sizes, within-group errors, units and consequences of failure. No deployment decision follows from this number alone. Visual purpose: show 90 easy cases | 10 difficult cases | Same 100-case total. Facilitation: ask students for a prediction before execution, locate the actual intermediate values, and distinguish observation from interpretation. title: Residual means prediction minus observation
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: Residual means prediction minus observation. Define: Positive means too high; negative means too low. Walk through: At x1=-2,-1,0,1,2, the noise-free square is 4,1,0,1,4. A deliberately fixed prediction of 1 gives residuals -3,0,1,0,-3. Ask: Which rows are underpredicted, and why? Expected answer and boundary: The two end rows: prediction 1 is below observed 4. This horizontal prediction is a declared teaching approximation, not a model fitted to those five points. Visual purpose: show Observed value > Predicted value > Subtract > Explain the sign. Facilitation: ask students for a prediction before execution, locate the actual intermediate values, and distinguish observation from interpretation. title: MAE and RMSE summarize different penalties
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: MAE and RMSE summarize different penalties. Define: Keep the same five residuals while changing the summary. Walk through: For residuals -3,0,1,0,-3, the absolute sum is 7 and squared sum is 19. MAE=7/5=1.4; RMSE=sqrt(19/5), about 1.949. Ask: Why does the larger error receive more weight in RMSE? Expected answer and boundary: Its contribution is squared before averaging. Neither metric is universally better: the loss should match the stated task and error costs. Visual purpose: show Absolute errors | Squared errors | Average | Response units. Facilitation: ask students for a prediction before execution, locate the actual intermediate values, and distinguish observation from interpretation. Transition: connect this checked mechanism to the next beat; preserve the lab artifact where requested. title: A straight model cannot draw a square
notes: 2 minutes / explanation. Teaching intent: A straight model cannot draw a square. Define: Scaling an input does not create a missing nonlinear feature. Walk through: Hold x0=0 and noise=0 for the visual slice. The fixed line predicts 1; the true curve is x1 squared. Explain their difference before fitting anything. Ask: Why not fix this only by standardizing x1? Expected answer and boundary: Centering and scaling are affine operations. They cannot create x1 squared. The five-point approximation is separate from the two pipelines we will actually train. Visual purpose: show Raw x1 > Center and scale > Still a line | Add x1 squared > Curved response. Facilitation: ask students for a prediction before execution, locate the actual intermediate values, and distinguish observation from interpretation. Transition: connect this checked mechanism to the next beat; preserve the lab artifact where requested. title: Task 1: predict, calculate, explain
